articles.title: Headteachers consider leaving jobs earlier than planned after new Ofsted inspection
articles.summary:
Almost two-thirds of school leaders polled say new regime is much more intense than previous framework

More than half of headteachers in England who were polled after their schools were…

blocks.text: More than half of headteachers in England who were polled after their schools were inspected under Ofsted’s new regime are considering cutting short their careers as a result of the experience.
In response to the question “Has the inspection affected how long you intend to stay in your role?”, 52% of those who responded said they were thinking of leaving their job sooner than planned.

Amost two-thirds (64%) said the new inspections were “much more intense” than under the previous framework, while nearly nine in 10 (86%) struggled with their mental health and wellbeing while inspectors were on site.

The findings from the survey by the National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) are a damning indictment of the new regime that is the result of a radical overhaul after the suicide of the primary school headteacher Ruth Perry in January 2023.
The changes, which were introduced a year ago, were intended to reduce the strain and workload caused by the inspection process, but many school leaders say they have made things worse.

One primary headteacher who took part in the survey said: “Not sure my physical or mental health could cope with another inspection like this framework. Have been a head for 15 years across three schools and have never felt less able to do my job than I did during the inspection.”

A deputy head at an all-through school said: “I previously had aspirations for headship. I will now never go for headship. The stress and anxiety of the inspection has ended that dream … this is the most challenging Ofsted I have ever completed in a career of over 20 years.”
A primary school chief executive said: “I’m very tired of the high stakes, the stress, the worry that comes from the whole process. It’s on a different level.”

A headteacher at a secondary special school said: “I will not do another inspection as head. I will leave before the next one – it made too much of an impact on my personal life – I didn’t see my children for months on the run up to going into window.”

The general secretary of the NAHT, Paul Whiteman, said the survey findings showed “the unmitigated failure of an unaccountable and out of control inspectorate” and said Ofsted’s actions were driving experienced leaders from schools.

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, has indicated she is looking at further changes to Ofsted, but Whiteman said that “another belated rearranging of the deckchairs which sidelines the profession is wholly insufficient”.

The survey, which had 242 responses between June and October, comes after teaching unions declared no confidence in the schools watchdog and threatened strike ballots unless significant wellbeing issues caused by the new inspection framework were fixed.
after newsletter promotion
An Ofsted spokesperson said many leaders had found inspections helpful and constructive over the last year, but acknowledged that others had highlighted the impact on their workload and wellbeing.

“That’s why we’re working with the secretary of state on ways to reduce the pressure felt by heads and teachers, without losing our shared focus on the best interests of children and their families,” the spokesperson said.
A Department for Education spokesperson said teachers do extraordinary work and inspections should support improvement without adding to pressures already on schools.

“That’s why we are working with Ofsted and school leaders to ensure accountability is collaborative, fair, proportionate and focused on helping every school get better, so every child gets the education they deserve.”

articles.title: LIVE: Sara Duterte impeachment trial, Nov. 10
articles.summary: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte resumes Tuesday, November 10, with the defense set to present its second witness as it seeks to dispute allegations that she failed to disclose…

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 8:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte resumes Tuesday, November 10, with the defense set to present its second witness as it seeks to dispute allegations that she failed to disclose properties in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).

Engr. John Kenneth Enumerables, the city assessor of the Island Garden City of Samal, is expected to testify on the tax declarations and tax maps of a property allegedly owned by Duterte's husband, Manases Carpio.

In an earlier hearing, the acting Samal register of deeds testified that Carpio purchased the property for P3.4 million in 2018. The House prosecution panel, however, said the property was not reflected in Duterte's 2019 SALN.

The defense is presenting witnesses and evidence to counter the allegations under Article II of the impeachment complaint, which accuses Duterte of amassing unexplained wealth and failing to truthfully disclose her assets.
Watch the proceedings live at 10 a.m. as the Senate impeachment court hears the defense's case.

articles.title: Court inspects Quezon City jail over alleged Romualdez irregularities
articles.summary: The court checked detention arrangements for former Speaker Martin Romualdez.

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 8:00am
Photo released yesterday by the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology shows former House speaker Martin Romualdez being guarded at the Quezon City Jail.

MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Third Division inspected the Quezon City Jail Male Dormitory in Payatas on Monday, November 9, following concerns raised over former House Speaker Martin Romualdez's detention arrangements.
The anti-graft court's Third Division, led by Associate Justice Karl Miranda, visited the facility operated by the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) on Monday afternoon.

"The Court is here today to conduct an ocular inspection of the Quezon City Jail Male Dormitory in connection with matters raised concerning the detention of former Speaker Martin Romualdez," the division said in a statement.
"The purpose of this inspection is to verify compliance with the Court's commitment order and determine whether established procedures are being faithfully observed," it added.
The court stressed that the inspection should not be viewed as a finding of any irregularity, saying it had reached no conclusion on the allegations or the conduct of any individual involved.
"The Court's responsibility is to ascertain the facts, uphold the law, and ensure that its orders are respected," the anti-graft court said.
The BJMP launched an investigation on November 3 after journalist Ramon Tulfo alleged in a social media post that Romualdez had been leaving the jail in an ambulance.
The Sandiganbayan Third Division also ordered jail officials to testify about Romualdez's detention and directed the BJMP to review CCTV footage and submit records on his movements.
Tulfo retracted his allegation on November 5, saying he had been given incorrect information.
Romualdez has been detained at the Quezon City Jail while facing a P7.44-billion plunder case linked to alleged kickbacks from flood control, infrastructure and other government projects.
The inspection also comes amid questions over Romualdez's access to a personal aide while in detention.

Quezon City Jail warden Maria Lourdes Pacion earlier confirmed that longtime Romualdez staff member Arvin de Guzman had been allowed to assist him with his daily and medical needs during visiting hours. She apologized for an earlier statement that gave the impression the aide stayed with Romualdez around the clock.

articles.title: Nvidia shareholders sue Jensen Huang over alleged spy ties
articles.summary: Nvidia shareholders have sued the chipmaker and its CEO, Jensen Huang, over his alleged ties to a suspected Chinese spy. The case adds to scrutiny over whether sensitive information at the AI giant…

image.caption: Huang led Nvidia's transformation from a gaming chipmaker into a central supplier of AI technology (FILE: 21/10/2026)Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Shareholders sued chipmaker Nvidia and its chief executive, Jensen Huang, on Monday, accusing them of concealing his alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.

The proposed class action adds to investigations into whether Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence, raising questions about the security of sensitive information at the world's most valuable chipmaker.
What does the lawsuit allege?

The complaint, filed in federal court in San Jose, California, alleges that Nvidia and Huang misled investors about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who is not related to him.
Shareholders say the defendants failed to disclose national security concerns that threatened Nvidia's reputation and business prospects. They are seeking unspecified damages.
The New York Times reported last month on the alleged relationship and said US authorities had concluded that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset.
What have Nvidia and Huang said?
Nvidia announced an independent investigation Sunday into reports that Huang had been the "target of a foreign intelligence effort."
Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in an open letter, but did not identify the woman.
Nvidia investigates CEO after reports of affair with Chinese spy
"I support the investigation and will cooperate fully," he said. "I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security."
Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% Monday. The lawsuit was filed five minutes after US markets closed.
How have Washington and Beijing responded?
US President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI was investigating the matter, while expressing support for Huang.
Trump said he had spoken to the executive earlier that day.
"He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," Trump told reporters.
China denied conducting an intelligence operation targeting Huang.
"The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.
Why does the case matter for the AI industry?
Huang co-founded Nvidia and led its transformation from a maker of gaming chips into a leading supplier of the computing technology powering artificial intelligence.
Its advanced chips have become a focus of US-China competition, with Washington restricting exports to limit Beijing's access to the technology.
Huang has pushed for looser restrictions on sales to China. The investigations have intensified scrutiny of his leadership and whether confidential company information was compromised.

articles.title: New trilateral talks on Ukraine war in Abu Dhabi: What to expect?
articles.summary: Ukrainian and Russian representatives last met in February for talks on ending the war, but the same sticking points remain. Ukraine continues to demand security guarantees, which is a non-starter…

blocks.text: A new round of trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States are scheduled to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, months after a flurry of US-mediated peace talks earlier this year in January and February went nowhere.

When announcing the new trilateral talks last week, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said the discussions would focus on "post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has named security guarantees, an energy ceasefire, unblocking the Black Sea, extended prisoner exchanges, and preparations for a meeting of the leaders of Ukraine, the United States and Russia as his key topics.
Lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia, a member of Ukraine's delegation, told DW he was not expecting quick progress.

"I don't think there will be a breakthrough, after there was such a long break in the negotiation process," he said. "Simply the fact that trilateral talks are being resumed can be counted as a success."
Who is sitting at the table?
Witkoff will be joined by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, real estate developer Jared Kushner, who serves as special envoy.

The Kremlin has sent Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, to act as chief negotiator, along with a delegation including high-ranking Russian military and intelligence officials.
The Ukrainian delegation will be led by Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, along with Arakhamia, and diplomatic and military officials.
Europe joins in
Separate formats are planned with several European representatives.

These include Günter Sautter, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's foreign and security policy adviser, Emmanuel Bonne, head of the Elysee Palace's diplomatic service and Jonathan Powell, the UK's national security advisor, and Fabrizio Saggio, diplomatic adviser to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
Björn Seibert, Chief of Staff for the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and Geoffrey van Leeuwen, Chief of Staff for NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, will also attend.
It's doubtful, however, whether European representatives will be formally involved in talks on a potential peace deal.
Hanna Shelest, a security studies director at the foreign policy network Ukrainian Prism, told DW she believed they'd play "an observing role, at best."

She added that, until now, Russia had been reluctant to have European representatives at the table to uphold the impression that talks were "a matter between two superpowers" — namely, Russia and the United States — and to increase pressure on Washington.
"I doubt the Russian delegation will let the Europeans have a say," she told DW.

"Experience from the past years has taught us that as soon as Medinsky heads negotiations, the point becomes demonstrating to the US that Russia is willing to talk, but in reality, they won't reach an agreement," she explained. "Instead, there will be a long sermon about history and all sorts of other things."
However, she said Moscow sending high-ranking intelligence officers as part of the delegation was a "fairly positive aspect" of Russia's intentions.
She believed that additional negotiations were possible at this level.

This could include over prisoner exchanges or humanitarian pauses in villages near Oleshky, a town in the Russian occupied Kherson region in Ukraine's south, where US First Lady Melania Trump was credited with arranging a temporary truce in late October that secured humanitarian aid and allowed civilians to evacuate.
But despite these "positive signals," Shelest cautioned against hoping for concrete results, and suspected Russia was using the talks to stall.
Oleshky truce as a template for wider ceasefire?
Late last week, Trump spoke of a "big beautiful agreement," after speaking with Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, "that might involve all of Europe."

This new security architecture, Kushner later clarified on social media, would be centered around "permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability."
These points "don't contain anything the Russians haven't been talking about since 2009," Shelest said.

Ivan Us, chief consultant and economic diplomacy expert at Ukraine's National Institute for Strategic Studies, pointed out that negotiations with people who are not decisions-makers could be simply for show.
But he agreed with other expert observers that negotiators in Abu Dhabi might try to use the temporary truce brokered for Oleshky as a model for other limited humanitarian ceasefires in the region.
But while Us said he saw cause for optimism, he also cautioned that Russia had continued attacks in Ukraine during the Oleshky truce, and had used the pause to fortify its positions around the town.
This article originally appeared in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Will Sara Duterte take the stand? Lawyer says 'too early to tell'
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte's lawyers are still weighing whether she will face the impeachment court herself.

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 7:30am
Vice President Sara Duterte shows a document after posting bail at a court building in Quezon City suburban Manila on September 5, 2026.
AFP / Ted Aljibe
MANILA, Philippines — It is "too early to tell" whether Vice President Sara Duterte will attend her impeachment trial or take the witness stand, spokesperson Paolo Panelo said Monday, November 9.
The trial resumed Monday morning after a nearly monthlong recess, with Duterte's defense beginning its presentation of evidence.
Saying "it is only the first day," Panelo said no decision had been made on whether Duterte would appear at the proceedings.
Whether the vice president attends or takes the witness stand would be a personal decision made in consultation with her defense team, he added.
Asked about Duterte's November 6 to 8 trip to Hong Kong, her lawyers said he was unsure whether the vice president had already returned to the country.
Duterte remained confident that her defense team "will disprove the allegations against her."
Panelo also denied rumors that Duterte would resign, saying the vice president "knows she is innocent."
The defense is presenting evidence on Article II, the sole remaining article of impeachment after prosecutors withdrew the other three.
The article centers on allegations of unexplained wealth, discrepancies in Duterte's asset declarations and her alleged failure to divest from business interests.
Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin was the first defense witness called to the stand Monday.
The defense has listed 24 witnesses for the November 9 to 13 hearings.

articles.title: Carney government spent over $19B on external consultants in its first year
articles.summary: The federal government spent more than $19 billion on external consultants last year, despite a promise to cut back on its use of outside contractors.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney campaigned on reducing spending on external consultants. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics
The federal government spent more than $19 billion on external consultants last year, despite a promise to cut back on its use of outside contractors.
Consultant spending nearly matches final year of Trudeau government
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 09, 2026 5:52 PM EST | Last Updated: 34 minutes ago
The government's audited financial statements for last year, released Friday, show the government spent almost $19.2 billion on external professional and special services in 2025-26.
That's almost as much as the $19.5 billion it spent on those services the year before.
Organizations contracted by the government last year include Bell Canada, KPMG, Microsoft Canada Inc. and the City of Toronto.

The Liberals have been criticized for years over how much they spend on outside consulting. Prime Minister Mark Carney promised in his election platform to significantly reduce the government's reliance on consultants, and to improve the capacity of the public service to hire in-house expertise.

In its budget, released last week, the federal government said it had already taken steps to reduce spending on external management and other consulting services by 20 per cent, in the hopes of reaching annual savings of $900 million by 2028-29.

Sean O'Reilly, president of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada (PIPSC), criticized the government for cutting public servants while not significantly reducing consultant fees. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)
Sean O'Reilly, president of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada, said while the federal government keeps promising to cut outsourcing, Canadians keep footing the bill.

"Actual spending in 2025-26 was barely lower than the year before, and projected spending for 2026-27 is the highest on record," he said. "The government is cutting its own public service experts, then paying a premium to rent that expertise back.
"That's not efficiency. That's waste."
Cuts to public service
The Liberals' 2025 budget outlined a plan to slash the public service by 10 per cent by the end of the 2028-29 fiscal year.
The federal public service has shed more than 23,000 staffers over the last two years, according to Canada's parliamentary spending watchdog.

An online tool released by the Office of the Parliamentary Budget Officer in September estimates there were 344,970 federal employees in the second quarter of this year, down 6.5 per cent from two years ago.

The government's financial statements show that the total spent on contracted services last year was $22.8 billion, which includes external contracting and contracts signed with other government departments.

items: Your questions about this year's federal budget, answered

blocks.text: The government's estimates show that number is expected to reach $26.6 billion in 2026-27.

The Public Service Alliance of Canada said in 2023 it negotiated language in contracts to protect public service jobs and reduce outside contracting. It also said the government had committed to a consultation process on the issues associated with contracting out in the federal public service.

The government and the Public Service Alliance of Canada are now again in contract negotiations. Among the union's key issues are job security and the need to end contracting services that it considers "wasteful."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Catherine Morrison is a reporter for The Canadian Press.

articles.title: Trump says Nvidia boss told him he had no idea woman he had affair with was Chinese spy
articles.summary: The US president said the FBI is now investigating the affair. He said he spoke with Jensen Huang and asked him about the affair.

blocks.text: Donald Trump has said the boss of Nvidia, whose affair with an alleged Chinese spy is being investigated, told him that he had "no idea she was a spy".
The US President said he spoke with CEO Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.
"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

Trump said the FBI was also investigating the affair. China has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia, who commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
Trump said the FBI was also investigating the affair but did not elaborate on the probe or when it was launched.
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.

articles.title: Canada can't control climate change on its own, economist tells landmark trial
articles.summary: The case was brought by 15 youth, who argue that federal legislation violates their constitutional rights by continuing the trajectory of greenhouse gas emissions.

image.caption: Julius Frauenheim, co-president of the UBC Environmental Policy Association, leads a rally in support of a youth-led climate trial in Vancouver on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. An environmental economist testified in the trial on Monday. (CBC News)

blocks.text: British Columbia
The case was brought by 15 youth, who argue that federal legislation violates their constitutional rights by continuing the trajectory of greenhouse gas emissions.
Multiple youth have filed lawsuit, arguing that feds are violating their constitutional rights
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 09, 2026 5:44 PM EST | Last Updated: 1 hour ago

An environmental economist testifying at Canada's first youth-led climate trial says the country has a limited ability to affect the climate inside its borders as it is largely determined by the choices of other countries.

David Anthoff, who studies climate change and environmental policy and is a professor at the University of California, Berkeley, is the first witness called by the federal government in the Federal Court trial in Vancouver.
The case was brought by 15 youth, who are arguing that federal legislation violates their constitutional rights by continuing the trajectory of greenhouse gas emissions.
Anthoff said Monday that Canada contributes about 1.4 per cent of global emissions.
"So Canada can have an impact on the global climate and an impact on Canada's climate by changing its own emissions, but it's relatively small compared to the overall size of the problem," he said.
"Most of the climate change that Canada will experience, whether that is large or not, will be determined by the choices of other countries outside of Canada."
Can you sue Canada for not doing enough about climate change?

Anthoff said it is not his view that "what Canada does doesn't matter," that it is futile or that there are no consequences to its emissions, but Canada would fare better if it managed a foreign policy initiative between several countries that agreed to a co-ordinated effort.

"Then something like that might be a much bigger lever than just the domestic greenhouse gases within Canada just because the vast majority of this problem is caused by emissions outside of Canada's border," he told the court.
Anthoff testified that mitigation policies require international co-ordination, while adaptation policies do not.

items: Supporters rally as historic youth-led climate trial begins in Vancouver
No catastrophic financial hit required to fight climate change, scientists say in landmark court case

blocks.text: He said mitigation policies that reduce greenhouse gas emissions "are meant to slow down climate change or solve the root problem."
"Mitigation outcomes are by definition a function of the choices of every country, and so effective mitigation policies will require some level of co-ordination or joint action to happen," he said.
Meanwhile, Anthoff said adaptation policies are actions or reactions people or states have to climate change, and can be done without co-ordination, within one jurisdiction.
"It could be a province that solves some of these problems by itself," he said.
Canadian youth launch climate lawsuit against federal government
Plaintiffs' case heard first
The plaintiffs' lawyer, Catherine Boies Parker, told the court in her opening statement the case was not about the existence of climate change.
Rather, it hinges on whether the government is "constitutionally required to stop making it worse," she said.

The plaintiff's case was heard first and included testimony from youth from seven provinces and two territories on how they have suffered "specific harms connected directly to the government's conduct."

items: Historic lawsuit challenging government over climate inaction begins trial hearings
Canada can 'definitely' transition to renewables by 2050, expert tells youth climate trial

blocks.text: BJ Wray, counsel for Canada's Department of Justice, told the court in opening arguments that the Charter was "never intended to solve existential crises," and that providing the plaintiffs with a safe climate system" is not something the country can do on its own.
The trial comes about seven years after the case was first filed in 2019. It is expected to continue into late November, with closing arguments scheduled for February.

articles.title: Todd Russell, Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor, dies aged 54 due to illness
articles.summary:
Tasmanian premier leads tributes for Russell, who earlier this month returned home to ‘see out his days’

  • Get our

blocks.text: Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor Todd Russell has died aged 54 after recently announcing deteriorating health.
The Tasmanian premier, Jeremy Rockliff, led the tributes on Tuesday morning, saying his thoughts were with Russell’s loved ones.
“Vale Todd Russell,” Rockliff wrote on social media.
“Thoughts this morning are with Todd’s loved ones and everyone who had the absolute pleasure of knowing him.”
Russell made global headlines in 2006 when he and co-worker Brant Webb were rescued after spending two weeks trapped below the surface at the mine in northern Tasmania.
The collapse killed miner Larry Knight, with Russell and Webb returning to the surface after a daring rescue mission almost one kilometre underground.
The pair were initially presumed dead after a rockfall before their faint cries from within a small steel cage were heard by searching workmates days later.
In 2025, Russell announced he had started treatment in hospital for an undisclosed illness.
Earlier in November, he announced he would return home to “see out his days” with friends and family.

“After years of pain, uncertainty, appointments, treatments, setbacks, and endless battles, plus the emotional exhaustion of having to pick myself up time and time again, have left me with nothing left to give,” he posted on social media.

articles.title: Canadian ultramarathoner Stephanie Case is the 1st woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica
articles.summary: Canadian ultramarathoner Stephanie Case completed the Antarctic Ice Ultra in Queen Maud Land, Eastern Antarctica, on Sunday, making her the first woman to run 100 miles, or 160.9 kilometres, on the…

image.caption: Stephanie Case, 44, at the finish line of the Antarctic Ice Ultra on Sunday in Queen Maud Land, East Antarctica. She's now the first woman to run 100 miles on the icy continent. (Jan Lenfert/Peak Pixel Cafe/The North Face)

blocks.text: Canada·New

Canadian ultramarathoner Stephanie Case completed the Antarctic Ice Ultra in Queen Maud Land, Eastern Antarctica, on Sunday, making her the first woman to run 100 miles, or 160.9 kilometres, on the southernmost continent covered by the largest ice sheet in the world.
Case, 44, crossed the line in 17 hours, 31 minutes and 39 seconds
She admits the race — in which she ran a 4.2 kilometre loop 38 times over 17 hours on the coldest and windiest continent on the planet — had her rethinking her life choices at times.

But Canadian ultramarathoner Stephanie Case still bested the Antarctic Ice Ultra in Queen Maud Land, Eastern Antarctica, on Sunday. That makes her the first woman to run 100 miles, or 160.9 kilometres, on the southernmost continent covered by the largest ice sheet in the world.
She carried a Canadian flag and cried happy tears as she crossed the finish line in 17:31:39. Her running shoes crunched and squeaked through the frigid packed snow.
"I knew roughly what I would be facing, but I had never experienced an environment as extreme as that before," Case, 44, told CBC News Monday.
"It feels pretty amazing to put women on the map there, especially in a place that used to be called the womanless continent."
Organizers call it the "ultimate test of human endurance at the bottom of the world." Runners have been braving icy temperatures in the Antarctic Ice Ultra since its inaugural race in 2024.
For safety reasons, the course is a 4.2-kilometre looped circuit around a basecamp — meaning those who completed the 100-mile ultramarathon ran the same loop 38 times plus another 300 metres.
Stephanie Case during the Antarctic Ice Ultra on Sunday. (Jan Lenfert/Peak Pixel Cafe/The North Face)

Case says she got into a rhythm, focusing on 10 loops at a time to make it a full marathon before stopping to warm up in the aid tent. Although on the first round, she had to stop after eight loops because her balaclava had iced up so much she couldn't breathe through it.
They also had to start racing at 1 a.m., the coldest part of the night, due to incoming storms, Case said.

Race organizers described Case's time as "blazing fast" in an Instagram post, adding it was "an extraordinary display of speed, strength and endurance in one of the most extreme environments on Earth."
She placed second overall out of 28 runners. Yusheng Ni of China won the race, finishing in 17:02:24.
Stephanie Case just after crossing the finish line. (Jan Lenfert/Peak Pixel Cafe/The North Face)
'Motherhood isn't the finish line'
This isn't the first time Case, 44, a former UN human rights lawyer who was born in Kingston, Ont., has made global headlines for smashing gruelling races.

In May 2025, Case won the Ultra-Trail Snowdonia in Wales, where she placed first among women with a time of 16:53:22 and went viral for the race photos where she breastfeeds her daughter, Pepper, who was six months old at the time.
Some of the attention was negative, Case says, explaining there were people who said she should be at home with her baby, and that she was selfish for training with a young daughter.

items: Canadian wins 100-km ultramarathon while stopping to breastfeed her baby along the way
A runner died in the New York City Marathon. Have the risks changed as more people race?

blocks.text: "I think that is completely the wrong narrative," Case said.
"Moms shouldn't feel guilty for prioritizing things that make them feel happy and whole — it makes us better parents in the end."
Ultrarunner Stephanie Case is pictured during the Ultra-Trail Snowdonia in Wales, where she came in first, on May 17, 2025. (Stephanie Case)
Now, Case says she's excited to go home to Chamonix, France, and tell Pepper all about her race. Pepper also watched her finish on the livestream, she added.
"I hope this shows everyone that motherhood isn't the finish line," she said.
"I was racing to prove to myself, and to anyone out there, that moms can do pretty badass things."

Next up for Case is the Arctic Spine, a 472-kilometre trail race in northern Sweden in February. She noted she will need to go on skis, pull her own sled, melt her own snow and pitch her own tent. And she joked that the extreme conditions in the Antarctic Race Ultra had her questioning her decision to sign up for her upcoming expedition through the Arctic tundra.
"I was rethinking my life choices out there during the race in Antarctica, I must say."
Stephanie Case pictured during the the Antarctic Ice Ultra on Sunday. (Antarctica Ice Ultra/Runbuk)
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: English author M. John Harrison wins the 2026 Booker Prize for The End of Everything
articles.summary: The annual U.K. prize honours best novel written in English from anywhere in the world.

image.caption: English author M. John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize for his novel The End of Everything. Harrison is the first sci-fi author to win the award. (Riverhead, Booker Prize)

blocks.text: Books
The annual U.K. prize honours best novel written in English from anywhere in the world.
Annual U.K. prize honours best novel written in English from anywhere in the world
English author M. John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize for his novel The End of Everything, a post-apocalyptic adventure that explores what it means to be human in a shifting world.
The £50,000 (approx. $94,893 Cdn) prize annually recognizes the best original novel written in the English language and published in the U.K.

The End of Everything is set in a slow-collapsing, near-future landscape along the Kent coast of the U.K. Years after an obscure, world-altering crisis, governments across the world barely function and the seas teem with strange new life.
Harrison becomes the first sci-fi author to win the award.

Harrison is an author and literary critic. He sold his first story in 1965, and in 1969 joined the staff of the U.K. speculative fiction magazine New Worlds, where he edited the books pages until 1978.

His novels include Climbers, which won the Boardman Tasker Prize for Mountain Literature in 1989; Nova Swing, which won the Arthur C. Clarke Award in 2007; and The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again, which won the 2020 Goldsmiths Prize for innovation in fiction.
A collection of short stories, You Should Come With Me Now, was published in 2017, and a volume of selected stories written between 1970 and 2020 was published under the title Settling the World.

This year's Booker Prize jury is comprised of poet, writer and educator Raymond Antrobus, musician, writer and broadcaster Jarvis Cocker, journalist, editor and critic Rebecca Liu and poet and essayist Patricia Lockwood.
The jury is chaired by English classicist, writer and broadcaster Mary Beard.

The shortlist also included Jamaican author Marlon James's The Disappearers, Scottish author Douglas Stuart’s John of John, U.K. poet and writer Luke Kennard's Black Bag, English writer Rebecca Perry's May We Feed the King and American author Elizabeth Strout's The Things We Never Say.
The six-book shortlist was whittled down from a longlist of 13. Shortlisted writers will receive £2,500 (approx. $4,692 Cdn) and a specially bound copy of their book.
There are no Canadians on this year's list.
Since 2013, authors from any nationality have been eligible for the Booker Prize.
In 2025, Montreal-born author David Szalay won the Booker prize for his novel Flesh.
Two other Canadians have won the prize since its inception in 1969: Michael Ondaatje in 1992 for The English Patient and Yann Martel in 2002 for Life of Pi.

articles.title: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
articles.summary: Jensen Huang is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

blocks.text: The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.

Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.
In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.
The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models.

"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.
Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand.
It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.
The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little.

But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.

For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech.
"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.
It think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.

The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.

We don't know when their affair began or ended, but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work.
China denies that she was engaged in espionage.

Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.

China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest.

Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.
Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy.

He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.

Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.
But can he survive?

At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.
Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.
An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.
And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out.
Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.

He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.

While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings.
And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

articles.title: Trial date of alleged Charlie Kirk killer set for June 2028
articles.summary: Tyler Robinson has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the 2025 killing of the conservative activist.

blocks.text: The trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk, will start in June 2028, a judge has ordered.
Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the September 2025 killing of Kirk, 31, who was shot while he spoke at a Utah college campus.

Utah County judge Tony Graf Jr on Monday told the court that jury selection would begin on 21 June, 2028. The prosecution has estimated the trial could last 17 weeks, while defence lawyers have said it could take seven months.
Robinson could face the death penalty if found guilty of aggravated murder, something his defence team has sought to prevent.
Prosecutors previously told the court they could be ready for trial by October 2027 but were willing to move that date back to January 2028 to avoid the holiday period.

But defence attorneys said they needed more time to prepare their case and floated a 2029 start. As well as trying to stop Robinson facing the death penalty, they have also tried to have cameras banned from the courtroom.

Kirk's widow, Erika, with whom he had two children, had pushed for as early a trial date as possible while also arguing proceedings should be live-streamed. She, along with Kirk's parents, ⁠Robert and Kathryn, have attended a number of court hearings in the case.

At the end of Monday's proceedings, Erica Kirk's lawyer, Jeffrey A Nieman, told the judge that while "a trial in the summer of 2028, three years after Charlie's assassination, does not feel very speedy to the Kirk family", they had "no choice but obviously to accept the schedule the court's put forward".
Nieman added: "The family has waited long enough already; they should not have to wait any longer for this."
During a five-day preliminary hearing in July, prosecutors outlined their evidence to show probable cause for trial.

This included DNA allegedly tying Robinson to the murder weapon and other items recovered at the scene; confessions he allegedly made to loved ones; and a taped video statement from his roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs.
"There is a mountain of evidence that proves that he is the shooter," prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court in September.

"We know that the defendant is the shooter… first, because of the video evidence; second, because of the DNA; third, because of his admissions; and fourth, because of circumstantial evidence," McBride said.
Defence attorneys, meanwhile, have cast doubt upon evidence and expert witness credentials in the case.

articles.title: Ottawa doubles maximum time employer can hire low-wage temporary foreign workers
articles.summary: The government said restrictions on hiring temporary foreign workers in cities with unemployment rates above six per cent will remain in place. But Ottawa is adding early childhood educators to the…

image.caption: Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Lena Metlege Diab says her department will work more closely with the provinces to ensure they can set the temporary foreign worker thresholds that meet their needs. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The government said restrictions on hiring temporary foreign workers in cities with unemployment rates above six per cent will remain in place. But Ottawa is adding early childhood educators to the list of professions exempted from those restrictions, which already includes certain jobs in health care, construction and food processing.
Minister says government maintains all jobs should be available to Canadians first
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 09, 2026 4:42 PM EST | Last Updated: 11 minutes ago
The federal government is extending the period of time a business can employ a low-wage temporary foreign worker.

The change will lengthen the maximum duration of a low-wage Labour Market Impact Assessment — the document an employer needs in order to employ a temporary foreign worker — to two years instead of one.

Ottawa is also proposing a series of additional measures for low-wage Labour Market Impact Assessment applications that are set to take effect on March 1, 2027. The provinces and territories would need to opt in to the changes in order for them to take effect.
These proposed measures include one that would allow the provinces and territories themselves to add or remove occupations from the list of jobs exempt from the six per cent rule.

items: Carney says new immigration levels plan is 'sustainable' as it draws ire of Conservatives
Tim Hortons commits to hiring 10,000 local employees, scaling back on temporary foreign workers

blocks.text: The federal government is also proposing that provinces and territories have the power to allow employers to expand the share of their workforces made up of low-wage temporary foreign workers to 15 per cent — up from the current limit of 10 per cent.
Immigration Minister Lena Diab said Monday the government intends to work more closely with the provinces and territories on tailoring the temporary worker program to regional needs.
"I have heard also loud and clear from many people across the country, no matter who they are, that there is a need for that program," Diab told a news conference in Stellarton, N.S.
Companies scramble to fill jobs as foreign workers leave Canada
Diab said while temporary workers' share of the workforce might rise in some fields, the government maintains all jobs should be made available to Canadians first.

"But we do recognize that we also need the skilled trades and the skilled people that have different skills than what we have in Canada, but also there are regions in the country that do not have the Canadians applying," Diab said.

"The percentages that you raise will be up to the provinces and territories to say yes or no. This is again working in partnership with the provinces in territories who will decide whether that is the right thing to do for their provinces, and if so, where in the regions."

items: Ottawa to allow rural employers to increase proportion of temporary foreign workers
Ontario rejects Ottawa's offer to let rural employers hire more temporary foreign workers
P.E.I. declines Ottawa's offer to let rural employers hire more temporary foreign workers

blocks.text: Diab was in Stellarton to announce that the Rural Community Immigration Pilot is being made into a permanent government program and a permanent residency pathway.

This program involved more than 1,950 vetted employers in 14 rural communities that faced labour shortages and couldn't fill jobs solely with local workers. The government helped those employers connect with skilled foreign workers who would then be put on a path to permanent residency.
About 5,500 permanent residency slots are assigned to this program in the latest immigration levels plan and the government says it plans to open the program up to more communities in the future.

The government alluded to temporary foreign worker program reforms in Thursday's budget. Government officials who briefed reporters on background Thursday said they did not have detailed information about the planned reforms — which were published the next day.
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Friday that the temporary foreign worker program should not be an option in communities where the unemployment rate is above 5.5. per cent.

The national unemployment rate was 6.7 per cent in October, according to Statistics Canada. The unemployment rate has fluctuated month-to-month between around 6.5 per cent and seven per cent for the last two years.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
David Baxter is a reporter with The Canadian Press

articles.title: Federal government budgets $12M for Justin Trudeau's archives
articles.summary: Canadian taxpayers could pay $12 million for former prime minister Justin Trudeau's records from his decade in office.

image.caption: Former prime minister Justin Trudeau speaks at an event during the Toronto International Film Festival in September. The new federal budget allocates $12 million over four years to acquire and preserve the files from Trudeau's time in office. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Canadian taxpayers could pay $12 million for former prime minister Justin Trudeau's records from his decade in office.
Multi-year funding comes as Library and Archives Canada scales back other functions

A single line in the federal budget tabled on Thursday reveals that the government has budgeted $3 million a year for the next four years to enable Library and Archives Canada (LAC) to "acquire, preserve and provide Canadians with access to the records of Canada's 23rd Prime Minister Justin Trudeau."

While Trudeau's official photographer, Adam Scotti, donated files to the federal agency, the archives has not yet acquired Trudeau's records, said Patrick Boissonneault, communications adviser at Library and Archives Canada.
Boissonneault said none of the $12 million would go to Trudeau.
There is an established tradition of prominent politicians donating their private records.

Typically, Library and Archives Canada assesses the material that is being offered and determines its monetary value. If LAC decides to acquire the records, the donor then receives a tax receipt for that amount, since the records are considered a gift of cultural property.
Boissonneault said the amount of the tax credit is considered a private matter between the Canada Revenue Agency and the donor.

Over the years, LAC has acquired the records of every former Canadian prime minister with the exception of R.B. Bennett, who served from 1930-35 and John Diefenbaker, who was prime minister from 1957-63, he said.
The cost of archiving prime ministerial papers has varied over the years.
"Past PM paper initiatives include $1.4 million for the records of prime ministers Brian Mulroney, Joseph Clark, John Turner and Kim Campbell," Boissoneault said.
The records from Jean Chrétien's decade in office cost $3.8 million while his successor Paul Martin's roughly two years of archives cost $1.7 million.
The archives spent $8.3 million to acquire, process and preserve the archives of Stephen Harper, Trudeau's predecessor.
Harper served from February 2006 to November 2015 — four months longer than Trudeau.
CBC News has asked Library and Archives Canada why the cost of the Trudeau archives is higher than Harper's but has not yet received a response.
Library and Archives faces budget cuts

The funding for Trudeau's records — more costly than Harper's, even when taking inflation into account — comes as Library and Archives has been hard hit by budget cuts under Prime Minister Mark Carney's government. In its most recent planning report, the archives said it has to reduce its spending by $11.1 million in 2026-27 and another $14.7 million in 2027-28 — the year the new funding for the Trudeau archives is set to begin.
A third cut of $22.1 million is expected for 2028-29.
By the end of the cuts, Library and Archives Canada expects to eliminate the equivalent of 161 full-time positions.

In the report, it says it plans to find the money by discontinuing the Documentary Heritage Communities Program, which helps smaller archives across the country, and gradually reduce its access to information and privacy (ATIP) functions and its proactive review of historical records.
"These changes to its budget and workforce will directly affect LAC's operations and its ability to fully deliver on its expected results," the archives wrote.
Former prime minister Stephen Harper's archives cost taxpayers about $8.3 million. (Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press)
The budget for Trudeau's records comes after Harper celebrated the launch of his records collection earlier this year.

Harper's records include 49.2 metres of textual records and 1.2 million digital photographs, sound recordings, digital moving images and video cassettes. They were the first time that a prime minister's records consisted of a large number of digital files.

During the event to launch Harper's collection, Jennifer Schofield, Library and Archives Canada assistant deputy minister of collections, said LAC invested considerable effort to preserve the records.

"We have a long-standing tradition of acquiring the private records of former prime ministers — photographs, audiovisual materials, paper files and in Mr. Harper's case, terabytes of digital records," she said.
Schofield said Harper's files "marked the largest digital archival acquisition ever undertaken by Library and Archives Canada at the time."

items: 20 years after his first election win, Stephen Harper steps back into the spotlight
Library and Archives Canada wraps up digitization of 6 million Indian day school records
Ex-PMs' archived papers include love letters, $500 — even a molar

blocks.text: Since leaving office, Trudeau has been travelling the world, carrying out a number of speaking engagements.
In September, he launched a new production company called Hope & Hard Work with his former chief of staff Katie Telford.

On Friday, the University of Oxford's Blavatnik School of Government announced that Trudeau was named a distinguished fellow and a member of the school's World Leaders Circle. Other members of the circle include former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern, former U.K. prime minister Rishi Sunak and former Colombian president Iván Duque.
In a statement accompanying the announcement, Trudeau said the challenges facing governments around the world require thoughtful leadership.

"I look forward to contributing my experience, exchanging perspectives with fellow leaders and engaging with the next generation of government and policy leaders as we consider how governments can respond to change and build a more hopeful, inclusive and prosperous future for everyone," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Award-winning reporter Elizabeth Thompson covers Parliament Hill & the federal government. A veteran of the Montreal Gazette, Sun Media & iPolitics, she works in the CBC's Parliamentary bureau, specializing in investigative reporting & data journalism. She's also a member of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists. Send story tips confidentially via Signal to ElizabethThompson.26

articles.title: Man who used fraudulent passport to get in and out of Canada 16 times handed 2-year sentence
articles.summary: A Ghanaian man who used a fraudulent Canadian passport to leave and re-enter the country 16 times has been sentenced to two years in prison for citizenship fraud.

image.caption: Jefferson Zormelo, 22, pleaded guilty earlier this year to violating the Canadian Citizenship Act by using a fraudulently issued passport to enter and exit the country 16 times. (Shutterstock)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
A Ghanaian man who used a fraudulent Canadian passport to leave and re-enter the country 16 times has been sentenced to two years in prison for citizenship fraud.
Jefferson Zormelo pleaded guilty to violating Canadian Citizenship Act
Jefferson Zormelo, 22, pleaded guilty earlier this year to violating the Canadian Citizenship Act.
On Monday in Calgary, Justice Karen Molle said Zormelo’s act “attacks the integrity of the Canadian citizenship regime.”
“The offence jeopardized public safety and our national security,” noted Molle. “Fraudulent use of Canadian passports affects Canada’s international reputation.”
With credit for the time he’s served since his arrest, Zormelo has about 14 months left behind bars.
Used airports in Montreal, Toronto, Halifax
Zormelo came to Canada on a study permit in 2021.

In 2024, when authorities determined he was no longer enrolled in school, an exclusion order was issued for his removal from the country, according to an agreed statement of facts filed as part of the guilty plea.

He then obtained identification documents, including a proof of citizenship under a false name, and used that to get a Canadian passport, which was issued under the name Mitchell Leblanc in December 2024.
Over the next 15 months, Zormelo then entered and exited Canada through Montreal's, Toronto's and Halifax’s international airports using the Leblanc passport a total of 16 times.
In April 2026, he was arrested by Canada Border Services Agency officers in Calgary after presenting a fake permanent residency card in the Leblanc name to officials at the U.S. Consulate.
Officers then searched Zormelo's hotel room and discovered, among other things, the fraudulent passport.
'Clever criminals pose a greater risk'
Prosecutor Tyler Lord had sought a five-year prison sentence.
Defence lawyer Devin Frank asked the court to consider a time-served sentence of nine months in jail, arguing his client experienced a difficult upbringing in Ghana, which involved poverty and abuse.
The judge noted Zormelo was "desperate to live and work in Canada."

items: Government abruptly suspends citizenship certificates issued under 'lost Canadians' law

blocks.text: In the end, Molle outlined a number of aggravating factors, including the fact that Zormelo used his intellect to commit the “sophisticated, elaborate” fraud.
“Clever criminals pose a greater risk to public safety,” said Molle.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Meghan Grant is a justice affairs reporter. She has been covering courts, crime and stories of police accountability in southern Alberta for more than 15 years. Send Meghan a story tip at meghan.grant@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Digong's defense wants ICC prosecution witnesses vs. Bato, killing quotas removed over 'speculative' accounts
articles.summary: PRAGUE, Czech Republic - The defense team of former President Rodrigo Duterte has pushed back at International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors over their bid to include two witness testimonies whose…

blocks.text: PRAGUE, Czech Republic – The defense team of former President Rodrigo Duterte has pushed back at International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors over their bid to include two witness testimonies whose accounts they allege to be based on “rumors, hearsay, and information obtained through media.”

In a redacted request filing released on November 9, Duterte’s counsel Peter Haynes asks Trial Chamber III to order the Office of the Prosecutor to remove P-1334 and P-1348 from its list of witnesses.

Haynes argued that the two witnesses – whose prior recorded testimonies are sought by prosecutors to be admitted in court under Rule 68(2)(b) – were “both absent for almost the entire period charged under Counts 2 and 3.”
“Accordingly, they can have almost no direct knowledge of how decisions were taken [REDACTED] or how operations were conducted during Mr Duterte’s presidency,” Haynes stated in the filing.
Striking out witnesses vs. Bato, alleged killing quotas

On October 26, Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang requested Trial Chamber III to admit the prior recorded testimonies and associated material from P-1334 and P-1348, whose evidence implicates former Philippine National Police (PNP) chief and incumbent Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa.
Their statements also allegedly mention “target lists of drug personalities” and “killing quotas and financial rewards” as well as establishing the roles in implementing Duterte’s drug war.

In the prosecution’s filing, P-1334’s evidence also relates to Incident 13 – or the shootout that killed former Albuera mayor Rolando Espinosa Sr., and Raul Yap, and Incident 53 – or the killing of an alleged drug pusher and another victim by PNP Anti-Illegal Drugs Group (AIDG) operatives.
Duterte’s defense rejected the prosecution’s assertion, saying the accounts of P-1334 and P-1348 were “substantially based on rumour, hearsay, and information obtained through the media.”

“She never saw Dela Rosa do anything of the sort, and recognized that her account is based on stories she had heard,” Haynes argued, citing the prosecution’s transcripts that currently remain unavailable to the public.

Stating several other reasons, whose substance remains obscured, Haynes said P-1334’s understanding of the alleged murder in Incident 53 is “limited”, and that claims she knew about Incident 13 “[come] entirely from newspapers or ‘people talking’.”
For P-1348, Duterte’s defense argued the witness’s prior recorded testimony lacks probative value, “given her inability to offer any direct information on matters of significance to the case.”
Haynes pointed out that P-1348 “cannot speak from personal experience” on the alleged killing quotas, and that “she accepted that her account is based entirely on hearsay.”

“In addition, her evidence appears to have been shaped by information obtained from news reports and social media concerning the nanlaban narrative, rather than by any direct familiarity with the events.”
Testimonies of “marginal value”

While Duterte’s lawyers “take no position” in the prosecution’s request to admit P-1334 and P-1348 under Rule 68(2)(b), they hit back at the opposing camp over introducing what they describe as “prior recorded testimonies of marginal value”.

“[These are] concerning matters said to support the contextual elements, but resting on a fragmented and increasingly attenuated chain of hearsay from unidentified individuals, ‘stories’, press articles and, more seriously, speculation,” Haynes said.

Other than asking Trial Chamber III to remove P-1334 and P-1348 from the list of witnesses, Haynes requested the court to admit only “those parts of the statements that relate to proof of matters other than the acts and conduct of the accused.”
He stated that “no reliance should be placed” on the prosecution’s application to include testimonies related to the following:

items: Duterte’s association with the Davao Death Squad (DDS) and drug cartels;
his alleged “targeting of mayors [REDACTED] who did not support him”;
his use of public funds to pay [REDACTED]; and
his public call for drug users to register in barangays.

blocks.text: Haynes’ recent filing is the latest bid by Duterte’s defense to strike out several prior recorded testimonies applied for by the prosecution under Rule 68(2)(b). The prosecution is seeking to admit these in court without the presence of witnesses.
So far, Trial Chamber III has not released a decision on the three prosecution applications.
Duterte is facing three counts of crimes against humanity and will face trial before the ICC on November 30, 2026. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case - media reports
articles.summary: The ruling means prosecutors can pursue the case, meaning they could reduce charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.

blocks.text: A Massachusetts judge has denied motions to dismiss the murder case of Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of murdering her three children, according to local US media.
The judge's ruling comes after Clancy's defence team requested dismissal of the case after her first trial ended in a mistrial in September, when a 12-person jury failed to reach a consensus.
The ruling clears the way for prosecutors to pursue the case. They could reduce the charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.
Clancy has not denied killing her children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional.
Clancy's defence team had filed three motions, including one to dismiss the case against her due to double jeopardy - a legal standard that says a person cannot be tried for the same crime twice.

Her lawyers argued that Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the August murder trial, acted prematurely when he declared a mistrial on 4 September, saying that he should have sought a viable alternative.
In his ruling on Monday, Sullivan said that a retrial would not unconstitutionally subject her to double jeopardy, according to Reuters news agency.
Sullivan also denied a motion to see records of the lone holdout juror in the case and to question the juror under oath.
The judge scheduled a hearing for 16 November to discuss when to hold a second trial. He has previously suggested it could begin in March.
