articles.title: France blames Iran’s Revolutionary Guards for cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges
articles.summary: French foreign minister vows European sanctions against Tehran over ‘unprecedented’ hacks last month

blocks.text: France has said Iran’s Revolutionary Guards were behind “unprecedented” cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges in the country last month, vowing European sanctions against Tehran.

“I can confirm that this attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” the French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, said on Monday of the hacks on 11 and 12 October.
“This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression,” he said, adding, “We will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack.”
Iran’s mission to the United Nations did not return messages seeking comment. Iran routinely denies carrying out malicious cyber operations.

The October hacks were followed this month by a second wave of hacking ‌that hit more than 100 establishments across Europe and even affected refrigerators used by French blood banks, prompting employees to move some of the blood to other cold storage units.

The seemingly straightforward nature of the refrigerator hacks – and their repetition ​across multiple countries – prompted speculation about who might be responsible amid ongoing concerns over Russia’s suspected sabotage campaign in Europe, the war between the US and Iran and the global rise of AI-powered cyberattacks.

articles.title: Labour’s Brexit red lines ready for ‘dignified retirement’, says their co-author
articles.summary:
Exclusive: MP Chris Ward believes ditching pledges and forming closer ties with EU would protect it from global threats

One of the architects of Keir Stamer’s Brexit red lines has called for…

blocks.text: One of the architects of Keir Stamer’s Brexit red lines has called for Andy Burnham to abandon them at the next election, saying a new relationship with the EU would protect the UK from global threats.

The call is the latest voice from a prominent figure in Starmer’s administration for a faster transition to a far closer European relationship, after the former chancellor Rachel Reeves said it was right for Burnham to consider rejoining.
Chris Ward, one of Starmer’s closest confidants in politics and one of the ministers who worked on the EU reset, said that it was the security relationship that meant a change was now imperative.

The Labour MP for Brighton Kemptown and Peacehaven said it was now time to give a “a dignified retirement” to the red lines, which rule out rejoining the EU, the single market, the customs union and restoring freedom of movement.
Ward also suggested there was little compelling argument for rejoining the single market without full EU membership, saying he had “never understood the argument for the latter without the former”.

But he said the main reason for abandoning the red lines was that the UK “could no longer rely on the Americans” which was a major geopolitical shift that merited an entire reappraisal of Britain’s diplomatic relationships. “That question was unthinkable in 2016, but it is unavoidable in 2026,” he wrote in an article for the Guardian.

Ward, who was Starmer’s chief adviser as shadow Brexit secretary and who co-authored the red lines in Labour’s manifesto in 2024, said that they had now outlived their usefulness and should no longer be part of Labour’s future thinking.
He remains close to the former prime minister and said that the drive to renew the relationship with the EU may prove the defining political moment of this autumn.
He said the party had agreed upon the red lines in the manifesto because they were “designed precisely to close down the debate and to narrow the target that Brexit had become for Labour”.

“I still believe that strategically this was the right course for Labour, and the reset deal that – touch wood – will get over the line at next month’s UK-EU summit will demonstrate that real benefits can be delivered within those red lines, whether cheaper prices for businesses, a youth mobility scheme or the return of the Erasmus+ scheme.

“By the next general election, however, those red lines will have served their purpose. They should be given a well-earned and dignified retirement. Frankly, they no longer speak to the world as it is in 2026, let alone as it may be over the years to come.”
Ward said it was well known that rejoining the EU or single market would have economic benefits but said supporters of rejoining should make a different argument.
“Pinning the case for a new relationship on old arguments risks both the same result and missing what’s really changed,” he wrote.

“Instead, its the huge geopolitical shifts and, above all, the new security and cyber threats the UK and Europe now face day in, day out that demand we now reassess the depth and nature of relationship.”
after newsletter promotion
He said Starmer had twice had to scramble alliances together – on Ukraine and on the strait of Hormuz – because “we could no longer rely on the Americans”.

“It would now be brave in the extreme to continue to pin our future security – and that of Europe – on the outcome of US elections, or the false hope that whoever is in the White House we can still bank on the US as we did in 2016, let alone 1945.”
Ward said there should be public debate on whether the UK should formally rejoin or seek a form of associate membership like Canada.

But he said the prime minister will “need to be clear as to why now is the right time to reopen the Brexit debate, what we are seeking, and why it is so important to our national interest. A re-run of the tired arguments of 2016 won’t do that. Defending red lines designed for 2020 won’t do that either. But appreciating the urgent strategic challenges of the decades to come just might.”
Burnham will attend the European Political Community summit in Dublin on Thursday, expected to be used to see Labour’s reset deal over the line and to meet many European leaders for the first time.

Burnham will also meet European leaders on the sidelines to set out his ambitions for further integration after he announced his intention to seek a closer and more permanent relationship – including potentially rejoining the bloc.
At a Brexit reset meeting on 20 November in Brussels, the UK will sign new agreements on agriculture and food, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.

The prime minister is then expected to give a speech after the summit on options for the future relationship. Burnham has said previously an option to rejoin the single market could be offered in a Labour manifesto but fully rejoining would need a referendum.

Known as the "DZ Mafia", the gang won a bloody turf war against a rival group in Marseille during 2023, and is now recruiting from further afield.
One member who is in prison awaiting trial after being implicated in several murders told the BBC he was part of a DZ Mafia hit squad.
He agrees the killings he has been charged with were "quite shocking".

"Attempts in broad daylight, in traffic jams… it can range from going to hit a guy, slap him to taking him in front of his mother and burning him up in a car. I think I have good composure, I handle it fairly well."
When challenged over whether he feels regret when carrying out such acts of brutality, he says he feels "guilty in-part" but claims to have no regrets.
Like so many teenagers from Marseille, he knew large sums of money could be earned quickly in drug trafficking. Now in his twenties, he admits the environment he entered was a "trap".

articles.title: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
articles.summary: The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up.

blocks.text: France has accused Iran of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers.
Speaking at a news conference, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of Iran.

He said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding that the country would "implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack."
The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up, which spoilt fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Then last week, dozens of supermarkets across seven other European countries were also impacted by a cyber-attack that targeted fridges and freezers. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Iran is yet to respond to Barrot's allegations.

Separately on Monday, the Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as well as his two deputies.
Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.

More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.

articles.title: Judo star Teddy Riner announces plan to run in France’s presidential election
articles.summary:
Five-times Olympic champion says he is neither leftwing nor rightwing but would seek to ‘bring people together’

The French judo star and five-times Olympic gold medallist

blocks.text: The French judo star and five-times Olympic gold medallist Teddy Riner has announced plans to run in next year’s presidential election, describing himself as someone neither leftwing nor rightwing but who would seek to “bring people together”.

With more than five months before the April-May ballot to replace Emmanuel Macron, the race has been shaping up to be a showdown between political extremes. Polls point to a hollowing out of the political centre, suggesting that the anti-immigrant National Rally leader Marine Le Pen could be the frontrunner, with the radical-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon trailing behind.
Riner joins a crowded field of candidates, with analysts describing him as a long shot, given his lack of experience and no party backing.
On Monday, he sought to position himself as someone who would unite people and bring “common sense, steadfastness, justice” to France.
“I know what people are going to say about me: ‘He’s crazy. He’s not from the establishment. He doesn’t have the codes. He’s never done politics,’” Riner said in a video posted on social media.

He listed the issues facing the country, from soaring debt to the rising cost of groceries and the precarious futures faced by those who don’t have the right network, family name or skin colour. “If refusing to bow my head and refusing the chaos makes me crazy, then yes, I’m completely crazy,” he said.

blocks.caption: Emmanuel Macron embraces Teddy Riner after he won the gold medal in the men's +100kg judo at the Paris 2024 Olympics. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

blocks.text: The announcement comes about six weeks after Riner, who has often been voted France’s most popular sportsperson, faced a wave of racist abuse and online harassment after telling a TV sports show he felt “anxiety” about the rise of the far right in France.
It also comes as the country has been rocked by protests over the cost of living, heightening the ongoing protests by schoolchildren over crumbling and crowded classrooms.

Riner, 37, who was born in the French Caribbean territory of Guadeloupe and grew up in Paris, cited his years of throwing and pinning down judo opponents to make the case for being elected president. “Fighting has always been part of me. I know what it’s like to fight, fall and always get up,” he said. “France does not need a professional politician who recites lessons and quarrels all day long.”
In an interview with the newspaper Le Parisien published on Monday, he described his views as neither rightwing nor leftwing.

Instead Riner, one of France’s most recognisable and popular athletes, pointed to broader issues. “The country is experiencing deep divisions right now, let’s not kid ourselves,” he said. “And in the face of that, I don’t see a single candidate putting forward a credible and fair vision capable of bringing French people together rather than dividing them. There is no one today offering genuine, sincere hope. It’s always one side against another.”

As Riner prepared to attempt to gather 500 sponsorship signatures from elected officials, as required by French law, he said some of his motivation to run came from those young and old who were finding it difficult to envision a future for themselves.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: France ‘allowed me to become the person I am today’, said Teddy Riner. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

blocks.text: “I hear the anger, which some people echo in their rhetoric with a great deal of negativity, coming from people who no longer have any ambition or the desire to think big,” he said. “Yet France is a great country. It allowed me to become the person I am today and gave me the opportunity to dream big. Today, that is precisely what is missing. There is no longer that ambition, no longer that hope.”
If elected, he said he was hoping to strike a balance between both careers so he would be able to compete in the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

He wouldn’t be the first judoka to embrace French politics: David Douillet was elected to the French parliament in 2009, years after his retirement from judo, later serving as the sports minister from September 2011 to May 2012.
Dani Podgoretskaya, an analyst at Eurasia Group, said there was little chance Riner would be seen as a serious contender.

“The French take the presidential election very seriously, given how much power the office holds. He has no experience in elected office, no party and no detailed programme yet,” she told Agence France-Presse. “While I still find it possible that we may yet see a providential figure emerge who unites the anti-populist vote, I doubt that Riner is that figure.”

When asked about his priorities on the world stage, Riner seized on the moment to crack a joke about potentially meeting the US president. “A lot of people around me have been talking about my first handshake with Donald Trump,” he said. With a laugh, he added: “We’ll see who has the firmer handshake.”

articles.title: Russia: Independent Novaya Gazeta shuts its Moscow newsroom
articles.summary: The investigative newspaper is closing its doors after Russian authorities labeled it a "foreign agent" and ordered it vacate its Moscow premises.

image.caption: Launched in 1993, Novaya Gazeta often took on Russia's criminal and political elites Image: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Novaya Gazeta newspaper closed its Moscow office on Monday, saying it was not able to continue reporting amid a campaign of state pressure in Russia.

The investigative outlet, co-founded by late USSR chief Mikhail Gorbachev, had long been a thorn in the Kremlin's side. In recent years, it ran into increasing roadblocks amid its critical coverage of the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
It was branded a "foreign agent," a Soviet-era term resuscitated by President Vladimir Putin's administration, with officials ordering it to vacate its Moscow offices.

Russian banks were also forbidden from processing donations from readers and supporters. The paper had been heavily dependent on this income stream after moving wholly into online publishing, with the transition taking place shortly after the invasion of Ukraine. Russian authorities introduced new wartime censorship rules in the wake of the full-scale invasion.

blocks.caption: Founding editor Dmitry Muratov shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize for his work with the paperImage: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nobel Prize winner Muratov calls for free speech
2021 Nobel Peace Prize-winning founding editor Dmitry Muratov issued an appeal for free speech in wartime Russia as journalists gathered in the Novaya Gazeta offices to witness its closure.

"Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today," he said. "We are currently at a point where the section of the Russian constitution that guarantees political and civil rights has ceased to function."

Russia's government meanwhile sought to play down the significance of the closure, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying it was part of a "rotational process" in a fiercely competitive media landscape.
What is Novaya Gazeta?

Novaya Gazeta was a flagship for post-Soviet democratic Russia and the era of "glasnost" or openness, also launched by Mikhail Gorbachev. The reformist Soviet leader used some of the prize fund for his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize as seed money for the publication.

The paper has built a reputation for fearless reporting, which has also put it in the crosshairs of Russia's wealthy and powerful. Six of its journalists were murdered since the paper was launched in 1993.

They included Anna Politkovskaya, who spent years investigating allegations of abuses by Russia's military during its campaigns in Chechnya. An early critic of Putin, she was found dead in her apartment bloc on the president's birthday in 2006.

Images published in Russian media on Monday showed the paper's editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, taking down photographs of Polikovskaya and other reporters murdered in what's thought to be retribution for their work.

blocks.caption: The paper moved online soon after Russia's invasion of UkraineImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Last month, when first announcing that the paper would close, Sokolov said the outlet had "been killed." The paper was shutting down after "the Russian authorities — the Russian special services — have forced the editorial team to end its work," he said.
Will closure in Moscow mark a definitive end?

Muratov called for a ceasefire in Ukraine and urged foreign observers to remember the strength of dissent that endured in Russia, even if it was being pushed underground by censorship laws and other repression or intimidation.
"We canot blame the citizens themselves for this," Muratov said, "especially the wonderful, truly remarkable younger generation."
"I urge you to distinguish between the Russian authorities and the Russian people," he added.
Muratov also called for the release of around 4,000 people he termed political prisoners in Russia.

Novaya Gazeta's leadership has not made it entirely clear whether its closing down in Moscow marks a defeinitive end to the outlet's reporting, or whether they might perhaps seek to regroup and begin operating in some form from outisde Russia, as several other publications including DW have been forced to in recent years.
One of its journalists, Irina Vorobyova, said that the paper's spirit would survive like a "good virus" and would "continue in everyone that was part of it."

articles.title: India’s demonetization: 10 years on, promises remain unfulfilled
articles.summary: A decade after the 2016 currency ban, its impact on India's economy and the fight against black money remains contested.

image.caption: Digital payments in India have expanded rapidly since the demonetization move in 2016Image: Amit Dave/REUTERS

blocks.text: On November 8, 2016, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced in a televised address to the nation that he was withdrawing all 500- and 1,000-rupee banknotes from circulation at midnight.
The surprise move invalidated 86.9% of the value of currency in circulation in a single stroke.
Modi asked Indians to make a "grand sacrifice for cleansing our country."

He promised that the hardship would help eliminate black money, corruption, counterfeit currency and terrorist financing. The exercise was presented as a major step towards a cleaner and more transparent economy.
The cost to the informal economy
Millions of Indians rushed to banks to exchange their savings. Long queues formed outside banks and ATMs, with people waiting for hours, sometimes without knowing when they would get their money.
Workers missed wages, small businesses struggled to pay employees and families found it difficult to buy everyday essentials. Reports of people dying during the cash crisis added to the distress.

"I still remember my domestic help's father," businessman Prakash Patra from Jaipur city told DW. "He panicked, collapsed, and passed away right there, standing in a long queue just trying to exchange his family's life savings. It wasn't just cash that was lost in those lines. It was human lives."
Is India ready to become a ‘global power’?

For India's most vulnerable, particularly rural women and people without bank accounts, the sudden cash shortage made savings difficult to access. Money set aside for family weddings, medical emergencies and basic survival was suddenly compromised.
Joe Athialy, executive director of the Centre for Financial Accountability, a financial watchdog, says the impact fell disproportionately on the poor and the informal economy.

"Demonetization destroyed livelihoods, disrupted small businesses and pushed millions into deeper economic insecurity. The poor and those dependent on the informal sector bore the greatest cost," Athialy told DW.

Arun Kumar, former professor of economics at Jawaharlal Nehru University and author of "The Black Economy in India," shared a similar assessment. The government wrongly assumed that illicit wealth was primarily held in cash, he said.
"And it penalized the cash-dependent informal sector while leaving the real engines of the black economy untouched," Kumar told DW.
Did it solve the black money problem?
The first major setback came in 2018, when the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) reported that 99.3% of the demonetized currency had returned to the banking system.
Only a small fraction of the withdrawn money had failed to come back, undermining the expectation that large amounts of undeclared cash would be extinguished.
India's AI ambitions: Can it become a global tech superpower?

A decade later, there is little evidence that demonetization made a significant dent in black money or corruption. Economists have long pointed out that much illicit wealth in India is held in property, gold and other assets rather than cash.

Some supporters of the policy argued that forcing cash into the banking system would help formalize the economy and widen the tax base. But the extent to which these changes could be attributed to the currency withdrawal remains contested.
Lekha Chakraborty, a professor at the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy, said research after the exercise pointed to limited success in achieving its stated objectives.
She draws on studies that examined both the immediate economic shock and its longer-term effects.

"The research points to modest gains against demonetization's primary objectives, alongside temporary but real economic costs. The impact was particularly severe in the informal sector, where cash remains central to everyday transactions," Chakraborty told DW.
"The economic shock was real, even if much of it faded over time. But there is little to suggest that demonetization produced a lasting change in the way black wealth is generated or concealed."
Athialy argues that the policy was based on a flawed understanding of how illicit wealth is held in India.
"Cash is only an insignificant part of the black economy. Much of India's unaccounted wealth is held in assets such as real estate and in tax havens, not currency," he said.
He also questions the absence of accountability for the disruption and its institutional consequences.
"Nobody has been held accountable for the economic disruption or the undermining of institutions such as the RBI."
Comparing mobile payment systems: India vs. Germany
Boost to digital payments
Digital payments have expanded rapidly since 2016. The Unified Payments Interface (UPI), launched in August that year, has become a major part of India's retail payment system today.
In 2025-26, UPI processed 241.6 billion transactions, worth 314.2 trillion rupees (approximately €2.95 trillion), according to the RBI.
Yet the growth of digital payments has not reduced the amount of physical currency in circulation.
RBI data show that the value of banknotes in circulation stood at 43.15 trillion rupees (about €405 billion) on October 23, 2026, compared with 17.97 trillion rupees (€169 billion) in November 2016.
The figures show that Indians are increasingly using digital platforms for everyday payments, but cash remains firmly in circulation.
Chakraborty cautions against attributing the growth of digital payments to demonetization. "Digital payments largely continued a trend that was already under way before the currency ban," she said.
A decade after the unprecedented move, the gap between the government's promises and what demonetization ultimately delivered remains central to its legacy.

articles.title: Ice hockey: Norway says it's been kicked out of World Juniors in favor of Russia
articles.summary: The wrangling over Russia's return to international ice hockey continues, with Norway saying it has been kicked out of the next major tournament – to accommodate Russia. Switzerland has joined a…

image.caption: The last time Germany hosted the World Championship in 2017, Russia won the bronze medalImage: Andreas Dick/Beautiful Sports/IMAGO

blocks.text: With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th (of 10) participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) said that the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had informed it that it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

The move, which has yet to be publicly announced by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to last month's Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision. The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued on Saturday, the IIHF said it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey."

As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta beginning on December 26. Still, Swiss Ice Hockey responded to Norway's statement, saying it's team would not face Russia at the World Juniors – as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.
However, it is far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," Mark Carney said.
"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

How this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the NIHF hope that its team could still play in the upcoming World Juniors. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.
"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten said.
"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days."
Hosts Germany continue to explore options

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed – or not – with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship next May.

"We intend to host the World Championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.
While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.
Lutz, who said he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility – if only as a last resort.
On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

"However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore — through dialogue — how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.
"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.
However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.
Could Munich's Olympic bid be a factor?
It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040, or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee – opening the door for their return to competition, despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.
The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games – like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) – to follow its lead.
Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius said he didn't wish to "speculate on implications."

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the issue could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

articles.title: ICC prosecutor: No issue with video testimony of witnesses
articles.summary: The prosecutor of the International Criminal Court does not foresee any issue with the audio-video link setup for some of the witnesses who will testify against former president Rodrigo Duterte.

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:00am
Former president Rodrigo Duterte attends the fourth status conference at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands, on Oct. 13, 2026.
International Criminal Court / Philstar.com's screenshot

MANILA, Philippines — The prosecutor of the International Criminal Court (ICC) does not foresee any issue with the audio-video link (AVL) setup for some of the witnesses who will testify against former president Rodrigo Duterte.

Acting prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang said this in response to the directive of the Trial Chamber III for the prosecution to address certain issues related to witnesses who would testify using AVL technology.
“The prosecution does not currently foresee any issues with respect to AVL testimony,” read Niang’s three page filing dated Nov. 6.
The filing also included a confidential annex containing the prosecution’s updated list of witnesses, as well as the number of those who will testify via AVL.
“The prosecution has marked which witnesses it anticipates may testify via AVL in the Updated List of Witnesses and has updated the anticipated calling order,” the prosecution told the judges.
“The prosecution will update the Chamber, parties and participants should circumstances allow these witnesses to testify in person,” it added.
The final number of prosecution witnesses has yet to be released.
During the case’s first status conference in May, ICC senior trial lawyer Julian Nicholls said as many as 70 witnesses may be presented against Duterte during his trial.
These include 31 insider witnesses, 17 crime-base witnesses and 12 witnesses “who are relevant to explain the background and the contextual elements of the crimes charged.”
The prosecutor intends to call 25 to 30 of these witnesses to give viva voce or verbal testimony during the trial.

articles.title: No guarantee of zero blackouts amid El Niño – DOE chief
articles.summary: The Department of Energy cannot guarantee that Filipinos will be spared from blackouts as a “very strong” El Niño threatens to strain the country’s power supply amid rising…

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Energy (DOE) cannot guarantee that Filipinos will be spared from blackouts as a “very strong” El Niño threatens to strain the country’s power supply amid rising temperatures.
“I’m not that confident because there are still red alerts,” Energy Secretary Sharon Garin told reporters yesterday when asked about the country’s power supply outlook.
The possibility of power plants going on unplanned outages or suddenly tripping also remains a concern, but the DOE is factoring in these risks, she said.
“We are trying to find other ways to temporarily bring in more power over the next three years to cover that contingency,” Garin said.
According to the state weather bureau, El Niño is expected to intensify into a “very strong” episode and persist until the middle of next year.

The prolonged dry spell could further strain the power supply as hydropower generation significantly drops due to reduced water levels. Electricity demand is also projected to rise amid hotter temperatures.

“Our estimate of the impact of El Niño is at least about 60 percent reduction in the generation of our hydropower power plants, and there will be disruptions in some of the plants due to extreme heat,” Garin said.
As part of its preparations, the DOE is accelerating the development of 200 power projects.
As of Oct. 26, 55 projects, including battery energy storage systems, had been completed.
It is also working closely with hydro stakeholders and concerned agencies to make the most of available water resources to meet both power and irrigation needs.
On the power distribution side, Garin said the DOE is coordinating with electric cooperatives to assess how El Niño would affect operations in their respective service areas.
“We want families to have peace of mind that hospitals and water facilities in their communities will continue to provide services amid El Niño,” she said.
20 senators seek calamity declaration

Twenty senators across the political divide, meanwhile, signed a joint resolution yesterday urging President Marcos to declare a state of calamity or imminent disaster in areas severely affected by the super El Niño.

Under Proposed Senate Resolution 765, the senators urged Marcos, upon the recommendation of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC), to make the declaration under the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010 and the Declaration of State of Imminent Disaster Act.

The senators called on the national government to mobilize resources to assist farmers and fisherfolk and to mobilize eligible funds under the 2026 national budget, including the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund and agency Quick Response Fund.

The resolution cited approximately P6.87 billion in agricultural losses affecting 249,028 hectares as of Sept. 26, equivalent to 43 percent of the losses recorded during the entire 2023-2024 El Niño episode.

As of Oct. 6, 106 cities and municipalities across Cagayan Valley, Caraga, Bicol, Calabarzon and Soccsksargen had declared local states of calamity, affecting approximately 388,375 people, according to figures cited in the resolution.
Closer monitoring of basic necessities and prime commodities to address overpricing, profiteering and hoarding in affected areas was also sought.
Schools to prepare
In the education sector, schools were urged to prepare for the impact of El Niño.

“Extreme heat, water scarcity, food insecurity and economic difficulties affect learners’ well-being, teachers’ working conditions and schools’ capacity to sustain learning,” the Catholic Educational Association of the Philippines (CEAP) said in a Facebook post yesterday.

The group recommended that schools conduct classroom and facility heat and water audits, establish accessible drinking water stations and schedule hydration breaks. — Marc Jayson Cayabyab, Rhodina Villanueva, Bella Cariaso

articles.title: Hontiveros seeks probe into pet crematorium scam
articles.summary: Sen. Risa Hontiveros has filed a resolution seeking a Senate investigation into the unregulated commercial pet service industry following the discovery of dozens of dead pets abandoned in a vacant…

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:00am

Philippine Animal Welfare Society executive director Anna Cabrera accompanies pet owners to the NBI on Nov. 3 to file complaints against Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium for alleged improper disposal of their deceased pets.
PAWS Facebook page

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Risa Hontiveros has filed a resolution seeking a Senate investigation into the unregulated commercial pet service industry following the discovery of dozens of dead pets abandoned in a vacant lot in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan.

Senate Resolution 762, filed yesterday, seeks a legislative inquiry into the alleged fraud involving pet owners who paid between P3,000 and more than P10,000 for cremation and other aftercare services.
The remains of 29 dogs and cats were found on Oct. 29 in Barangay Minuyan, stuffed into sacks labeled with their names and weights.
The Philippine National Police (PNP) had recorded 250 affected pet owners as of Nov. 4.

Hontiveros’ resolution also cited previous incidents in the same area, including sacks of dead dogs found in a septic tank in November 2025, 14 dead dogs discovered in May 2026 and more remains recovered from an abandoned pit on Nov. 3.

She stressed the urgency of establishing strict regulations to protect families, noting that Filipinos spent an estimated P95 billion on their pets in 2023, with 14.2 million households keeping companion animals.

The Bulacan police, led by acting provincial director Col. Jay Baybayan, said they had intensified monitoring, tightened checkpoints and deployed mobile patrols in strategic areas to help prevent similar incidents and identify those involved.
The police are also coordinating with local government units and other authorities to support the investigation and ensure that those responsible are held accountable under applicable laws.
P500K fine, jail time proposed

Meanwhile, a bill filed in the House of Representatives seeks to impose a maximum fine of P500,000 and up to four years in prison on pet crematorium operators who knowingly dump animal remains or misrepresent communal cremation as individual cremation.
House Bill 11785, filed by FPJ Panday Bayanihan party-list Rep. Brian Poe, seeks to regulate pet aftercare services, including cremation and burial, and establish penalties for violations.
Offenders would face fines ranging from P100,000 to P500,000, imprisonment of one to four years or both.
Poe filed the measure following the Bulacan pet crematorium reports.

Actor John Arcilla, who joined Poe at the bill’s presentation along with representatives of the Animal Kingdom Foundation and two pet owners who reportedly fell victim to a pet crematorium in Cavite, said he had his 11 dogs cremated.
He said he was distressed to think that the urns for his pets that he had kept beginning in 2004 might contain ordinary ash or, worse, manure.

“This is not just a piece of toy. We have a serious relationship with our pets, which is why we have given them that kind of decent burial or cremation, because we want to cherish and value our relationship with them,” he added.

“We are all victims here. We are calling on those who love their pets to go out and make noise. Our officials need to see our strength as a whole or in general. This issue has to be resolved sooner rather than later,” Arcilla said. — Ramon Efren Lazaro, Delon Porcalla

articles.title: Expect P16.80/liter gas price cut today
articles.summary: Motorists are in for some relief as major pump price rollbacks take effect across the board today, with gasoline prices dropping by at least P16.80 per liter.

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:00am
An attendant puts a fuel pump handle back in its cradle at a gas station in Paco, Manila, in this file photo from January this year.
Edd Gumban
MANILA, Philippines — Motorists are in for some relief as major pump price rollbacks take effect across the board today, with gasoline prices dropping by at least P16.80 per liter.
Diesel and kerosene prices will also see substantial reductions, with minimum rollbacks of P4.10 and P3.70 per liter, respectively.
Energy Secretary Sharon Garin attributed the steep price cuts to declining global crude oil prices amid easing tensions between the United States and Iran.

The rollback also reflects market reactions to the US midterm elections, where sweeping Democratic party victories against President Donald Trump’s Republican Party eased fears of a further escalation of the Iran war.
“What’s happening in other countries likely affects international fuel prices and hence, petroleum prices here in the Philippines are affected,” Garin told a media briefing yesterday.
She, however, said it could take time before domestic pump prices return to pre-war levels, noting the peso’s depreciation against the dollar is adding upward pressure on fuel costs.
As a net oil importer, the Philippines remains vulnerable to fluctuations in global oil prices, particularly amid persistent geopolitical uncertainties.

Energy Undersecretary Alessandro Sales, meanwhile, said state-run Philippine National Oil Co. remains committed to its plan to build fuel storage facilities with a combined capacity of up to one million barrels.
The first storage tank with a capacity of 180,000 barrels is targeted for completion before the end of 2027.

articles.title: SEC confirms data breach on its digital platforms
articles.summary: The Securities and Exchange Commission has confirmed a data breach on users of its digital platforms.

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:00am

In an advisory, the SEC said the accounts of its digital platform users “may have been leaked potentially through malware infection or unauthorized access by a third-party threat actor of your laptop, desktop, mobile phone or any other device you used to access our digital platforms.”
Businessworld / Aldrine Ballesteros
MANILA, Philippines — The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has confirmed a data breach on users of its digital platforms.
The agency did not provide any information as to how it ascertained the potential source of the issue.
It sent the notice to affected users days after cybersecurity advocacy group Deep Web Konek flagged a possible data breach involving SEC-related user accounts.
Last week, the SEC said it is treating the claims “with utmost urgency and importance.”
“The SEC is conducting a thorough investigation of the matter and enforcing enhanced security measures together with heightened monitoring of its systems,” it added.
The agency has yet to release the total number of affected users and maintained that no passwords in its databases were leaked or that no data was modified or altered in any way.
It said that no company records were involved in the issue.

“The categories of potential information that may have been exposed are strictly limited to: full name, username, email address, mobile number, date of birth, gender, address and TIN (tax identification number) of your individual account,” the advisory said.
Upon discovering the issue, the SEC said its technical response teams immediately initiated containment and preventive protocols, including formally notifying the National Privacy Commission.
It said “comprehensive security scans and log analyses were also initiated across all digital infrastructure to determine if any internal system showed signs of unauthorized access.”
“We further reinforced access controls, updated authentication credentials and verified data integrity to ensure no data modification occurred and corporate data assets remain secure,” it added.
The SEC advised affected users to implement security measures, including changing passwords and running a full security scan on personal devices.
“Be cautious of unexpected emails, calls or text messages asking for your personal or account information. The SEC will never ask for your passwords or security PINs,” it said. — Richmond Mercurio

articles.title: Macalintal to challenge SC ruling on BSKE postponement
articles.summary: Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal will ask the Supreme Court to review its decision upholding the constitutionality of the law that fixed a five-year term for barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan…

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal will ask the Supreme Court to review its decision upholding the constitutionality of the law that fixed a five-year term for barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials and postponed the BSK elections to 2028.

“I cannot – and will not – fail the Filipino people now. I am preparing to file my Motion for Reconsideration and will reiterate my plea for oral arguments to expose the grave errors in the majority ruling,” Macalintal said in his statement yesterday.

He added he would ask the high tribunal to schedule oral arguments for his petition, where he would “prove… that the postponement was deliberate and ‘intentional,’ a calculated move to deprive citizens of our fundamental right to vote and choose our leaders.”
The majority decision – penned by then associate justice and now Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda – ruled Republic Act 12326 was a term-fixing law and not an election postponement law.

Macalintal asserted, “If this ruling remains uncorrected, and if no one stands up to warn of its dangerous consequences to our democratic system, RA 12326 will not stop at the barangay level. It could embolden legislators to tamper with the May 2028 presidential elections under the guise of invoking the phrase ‘unless otherwise provided by law’ in Article VII of the Constitution.”
He believes the high tribunal may consider reversing its decision to uphold the constitutionality of the said law, which garnered a vote of nine concurring, five dissenting and one “on leave.”

“With five justices already voting in favor of my petition, I only need two more justices to reconsider their positions… From a 9-5 defeat, I earnestly hope and pray for an 8-7 reversal in our favor upon reconsideration of the decision,” Macalintal said.

In an interview over dzBB yesterday, Macalintal proposed a “win-win solution” wherein the SC could declare as constitutional the term-fixing power of Congress in RA 12326 and at the same time invalidate the law’s provision on election postponement.
Meanwhile, election watchdog National Movement for Free Elections yesterday urged Congress not to further postpone the BSKE. — Rhodina Villanueva

articles.title: Marcos swears in Zalameda, stresses speedy justice
articles.summary: President Marcos yesterday emphasized the importance of an independent judiciary and speedy disposition of justice as he administered the oath of newly appointed Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda.

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:00am
President Marcos swears in Rodil Zalameda as Chief Justice at Malacañang on November 9, 2026.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos yesterday emphasized the importance of an independent judiciary and speedy disposition of justice as he administered the oath of newly appointed Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda.
Zalameda, who succeeded retired chief magistrate Alexander Gesmundo, took his oath of office at Malacañang.
“If the resolution of a case drags on, it does not only waste time. It also adds anxiety and waiting time to families who are seeking justice,” Marcos said in a Facebook post.
The Chief Executive highlighted ongoing efforts to fast-track the resolution of cases and to ensure that Filipinos are treated fairly while respecting the independence of the judiciary.

“The President emphasized the importance of a strong, independent and accessible judiciary in upholding the rights of every Filipino and ensuring that the rule of law is upheld,” the Presidential Communications Office said in a statement.
“This includes strengthening trial courts, modernizing court services, promoting accountability and maintaining integrity and impartiality in the administration of justice,” it added.
Zalameda served as associate justice of the Court of Appeals for 11 years before his appointment to the Supreme Court in 2019.

The country’s top magistrate has been in the legal practice for more than 30 years, having worked as branch clerk of the Makati City Regional Trial Court, private law practitioner, public prosecutor, city prosecutor of Mandaluyong, presiding justice of the Court of Appeals’ 17th Division and SC associate justice.

Prior to his appointment as chief justice, critics questioned his independence, pointing out that he penned the SC decision that reversed the conviction on seven counts of graft of Marcos’ mother Imelda.
Malacañang has expressed optimism that Zalameda would be impartial, noting that he has extensive legal experience.

His appointment has drawn controversy, with critics pointing out that he penned the SC decision this year reversing the conviction of Marcos’ mother Imelda on seven counts of graft related to the Swiss bank deposits that were returned to the Philippines after being deemed ill-gotten by the SC in 2003.

articles.title: Fake news in Africa: In an age of disinformation, who decides what's true?
articles.summary: From Ghana to Mozambique, the fight against fake news keeps gaining momentum. But combating disinformation also requires safeguards for free speech, leaving some governments in an inconvenient…

image.caption: In junta-run countries like Burkina Faso, fact-checking initiatives like Fasocheck are under increased government scrutinyImage: Boureima Salouka/DW

blocks.text: Misinformation poses a threat to democracy worldwide: An exaggerated WhatsApp message, a manipulated TikTok video or an apparent breaking news alert on Facebook can all misguide people in Africa and beyond — particularly in the run-up to elections.

As artificial intelligence is making it increasingly easy to manipulate images, voices and videos, more and more countries are trying to equip their populations with skills to identify and counter fake news.

But are these efforts really about raising awareness, or are certain governments using this fight to control public opinion, silence dissident voices and misguide the populace — from both within and outside of these respective nations?
Civil society groups fill gaps left by governments

Journalism lecturer Dani Madrid-Morales at the University of Sheffield believes that African governments must significantly step up their efforts to combat sources of disinformation and misinformation.
He told DW that "there are very few countries — if any — that are actually doing a good job" to beat the influence of fake news.

blocks.caption: Dani Madrid-Morales believes that civil society has an important role to play in fighting disinformationImage: Privat

blocks.text: Meanwhile, he also points out that there also are civil society initiatives in various African nations which help inform people about the dangers of such false narratives.

For instance in South Africa, organizations like Africa Check and Media Monitoring Africa work together to highlight the impact of fake news on elections. Similar coalitions also exist in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Senegal.

However, these initiative mostly focus on fighting disinformation during election periods; the rest of the time, they typically lack funding and sustained engagement with civil society to continue to make a change.
When African governments become part of the problem
There also are deliberate efforts by certain governments not to battle fake news; some let it happen while others engage in deliberately spreading this.

Madrid-Morales distinguishes between three types of disinformation within this context: There are scams and similar schemes, which some governments, he says, fail to sufficiently fight, leaving people susceptible to financial losses.
He adds that there also are certain foreign influence operations trying to impact public opinion from outside a country and, in many instances, outside of the continent.
Finally, there are political disinformation campaings which originate from within a country, he explains.
"Governments are particularly interested in the third category," says Madrid-Morales, adding that this is particularly prevalent in the Sahel region.
He highlights how in nations like Burkina Faso and Mali, military governments have shut down media outlets, prosecuted journalists and expelled foreign correspondents to silence free speech.
In his view, these junta governments are primarily concerned with preventing negative or false information about themselves from circulating.
Why we need fact-checking more than ever
Do outside forces shape public opinion in Africa?
Foreign powers meanwhile also appear to play a considerable role in shaping public opinion across the continent.
Afrobarometer, a pan-African research network, examined the influence of international actors in terms of their influence over the continent.
The study found that over 60% of respondents viewed China's political and economic influence positively; this was followed by 52% for the United States.

Both countries have no past colonial history in Africa, although they are now vying for economic gains while focusing on infrastructure projects — partly to maintain this largely benevolent perception.

However, perceptions of other former colonial powers varied notabbly depending on factors such as the impact of past injustices: For example, in French-speaking countries, only 34% of respondents viewed France's ongoing influence positively.

Komi Amewonou from Afrobarometer meanwhile told DW that such attitudes are not necessarily the result of targeted propaganda campaigns but rather of African governments letting negative perceptions simpy run their course.

blocks.caption: Komi Amewonou stresses the dangers of foreign powers also influencing public opinion across AfricaImage: Africa-Fact Summit 2026

blocks.text: The mixed role of media literacy initiatives
In some countries, there are media development project trying to educate people and animate them to think for themselves.
Ghana, the NGO Penplusbytes runs the "Caravan of Hope" — a project supported German development agency GIZ and the by DW Akademie.

This mobile campaign brings media literacy training to rural communities through theater, role-playing exercises, public discussions and videos in local languages. The initiative has managed to reach 3,000 people in five districts to date.
The campaign also involves trusted community figures, as studies show that locals mostly trust people they know personally — particularly traditional village leaders and community representatives.

Rebecca Avusu from Penplusbytes, who helped develop the project, told DW that "information must be verified before people believe it or pass it on. This is particularly important for those without smartphones or with limited formal education."

blocks.caption: This event in the village of Odomase is part of the "Caravan of Hope" media literacy projectImage: Penplusbytes

blocks.text: Initiatives in South Africa take a similar approach: The country is home to Africa Check — one of the continent's best-known fact-checking initiatives.
The organization visits schools and teaches classes how to identify manipulated images, verify sources and deal with misinformation circulating in WhatsApp groups.

However, Madrid-Morales says that there can be a downside to such media literacy programs as well; pointing to research conducted in South Africa, he highlights that while some young people do become more discerning consumers of information, others eventually lose trust in almost every source, resulting in a complete lack of knowledge about important developments.
Limited powers elsewhere in Africa
In other parts of the continent, there's greater resistance against such media literacy initiaves — chiefly by their own governments.

In 2026, the International Media and Information Literacy Institute (IMILI) was opened in the Nigerian capital Abuja under the auspices of UNESCO, with a mission is to promote research, training and international cooperation in media literacy initiatives.

The government has said that it aims to play a leading international role in Africa in the fight against fake news; however, civil rights groups say the state often blurs the line between genuinely battling disinformation and silencing public dissent in the country.

blocks.caption: Rebecca Avusu, project coordinator of "Caravan of Hope" incorporates local leaders in media literacy projectsImage: privat

blocks.text: In Kenya, there are similar concerns: The Media Council of Kenya has the role of supporting journalists and fact-checking initiatives.

However, it's scope of operations is limited, as the organization abides by the country's laws to remain in operation — in particular legislation supposedly designed to target the spreading of false information.
Conversely, these laws have come under increased scrutiny, as they can also be abused the silence views against the government.
Madrid-Morales says that in such contexts, there need to be independent oversight bodies to ensure that people do not refrain from expressing themselves publicly for fear of reprisal.
Mozambique: Fighting disinformation as a tool of control

Meanwhile in Mozambique, the media institute MISA has also launched a series of fact-checking initiatives such as MISACheck. The program is designed to train young journalists and social activists in fact-checking techniques.
Olivia Massango, the vice-president of MISA, says however that the efforts of such civil society groups may seem like a drop in the ocean.

Massango is particularly critical of how state authorities deal with misinformation: "When something becomes inconvenient, the government ... invokes public interest, but ultimately often ends up protecting only what suits it, or what it finds troubling," she told DW.
As an example, she cites an internet blackout justified on the grounds of protecting public safety.
"Combating disinformation must not mean criminalizing opinions, criticism or journalistic work," she warns.

blocks.caption: Olivia Massango highlights that governments can abuse fake news initiatives to suppress press freedomImage: Privat

blocks.text: Guidance from Europe — with limited safeguards
More and more African nations meanwhile are turning to Europe in hopes of adopting mechanisms to fight fake news.

Morocco and Senegal are among the examples where proposed legislation is inspired by EU standards. Madrid-Morales however stresses that while following strong EU legislation in the battle against disinformation, there also need to be independent oversight and enforcement mechanisms to make them work.
In the cases of Senegal and Morocco, these are yet to be established.

Rebecca Avusu is also concerned about such efforts maintaining loopholes to suit governments is and as needed: "We do not want laws designed to combat disinformation to become instruments for silencing people who question government decisions or express legitimate opinions," Avusu warns.
A journalist's guide to spotting fake news

articles.title: Polish prosecutors say ‘too early’ to tell if Kraków gunman was motivated by political ideology
articles.summary:
Terrorism investigation will continue after suspect who killed six after opening fire in market square died

Polish prosecutors have said they do not currently have any evidence tying the man…

blocks.text: Polish prosecutors have said they do not currently have any evidence tying the man who killed six people and injured 16 in a rare mass shooting in Kraków to any particularly political ideology.

The 24-year-old Polish national died in hospital early on Monday after being critically injured in a shootout with police officers as they apprehended him after the attack in the city’s busy market square on Saturday afternoon.

Soon after the attack, the bodies of the gunman’s parents and sister were found at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a town about 100 miles north-east of Kraków. Police said they had probably died of gunshot wounds.

Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said on Saturday that the gunman, named in multiple reports as Michał Oksiński, was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views.

Polish prosecutors opened a terrorism investigation, which the justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, said would continue despite the gunman’s death and would aim to establish if he had acted alone or had been inspired by any group.
However, at a press conference on Monday, prosecutors said that there was no evidence tying the suspect to any particular political bent.

“We do not have findings that we could, in a responsible way, categorically state that he was inspired by any particular ideology,” the national prosecutor’s office spokesperson, Przemysław Nowak, said.
“It is far too early to comment on the motives … We have not found any obvious symbols that are generally associated with a particular political movement, whether far right or far left,” he added.
An interior ministry spokesperson told Polish radio that the “many emblems and patches” on Oksinski’s clothing were being analysed as part of the investigation.

blocks.caption: A view of the empty square after the attack. Photograph: Omar Marques/Getty Images

blocks.text: Żurek also called for “restraint” earlier on Monday amid the ongoing investigation. “Evidence is ​being collected, ​but I will not ​show or disclose it. I ask for restraint,” he told Radio ‌Zet.

blocks.caption: Candles and flowers are placed in the market square in Kraków after the shooting. Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/Reuters

blocks.text: Wearing military-style clothing and a bulletproof vest, the gunman drove at high speed into the square in the heart of the old town, which is usually packed with tourists, and started shooting at random in a “wild ride” around the square, Kraków police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło said.

blocks.caption: A bullet hole at the scene of the shooting. Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The shooting has shocked a country that had been considered safer than many of its European neighbours, and has deepened concern after several school stabbings in October that left one woman dead and which officials said were linked to extremist content online.
Among the six victims were a 32-year-old British man and an Austrian woman aged 51. The other four victims were Polish nationals.

Of the 16 injured, 15 were in a stable condition as of late Sunday, including two police officers who were brought out of medically induced comas earlier in the day. Five of the injured were from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia.

blocks.caption: Chairs lie scattered across a cafe terrace in the square the day after the shootings. Photograph: Beata Zawrzel/AP

blocks.text: Police said the suspect, who had no criminal record and held a firearms licence, initially continued shooting even after he was wounded by police during the exchange of fire. The two injured police officers – Jakub Kulik, a former paratrooper and volunteer firefighter, and Artur Morański– were hailed as heroes for their rapid response and for preventing further casualties.
Police confirmed on Sunday that three people found dead at the gunman’s home were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21.

Mourners have left candles in tribute to the victims in the square, which reopened late on Sunday. Flags across the country were lowered to half mast during two days of national mourning, as were European flags outside the European Commission in Brussels “in solidarity with the Polish people”, the commission said.

articles.title: Turkey: Workers killed in Izmir steel plant blast
articles.summary: At least 10 workers lost their lives in an explosion at a steel factory in Izmir, with the Turkish authorities warning more people are trapped under the debris.

image.caption: An eyewitness said the Izmir blast felt similar to an 'earthquake'Image: Servet Ulku/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: An explosion and fire at a factory in western Turkey left 10 workers dead, while rescuers searched for four more believed to be trapped under the debris.

The blast took place at the HABAS steel plant in Aliaga, in the port city of Izmir. The city's governor Suleyman Elban told reporters that 15 people were injured, two of them critically, and that further search and rescue efforts were underway.
The plant's production line was in the middle of a shift change rather than active production, according to the governor. Only some 200 workers were present instead of the expected 300.

An earlier statement from the governor's office said that the blast happened around noon (09:00 GMT) when an overhead crane toppled into a furnace during the casting of liquid steel. It also said that the authorities were investigating the incident.
Izmir mayor fears death toll could rise
Mayor Cemil Tugay wrote on X that the initial fire following the blast had been extinguished, but the exact number of dead and injured would become clear only after the debris had been cleared.
Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci, announced that those injured in the incident have been taken to hospital and their condition is being closely monitored.

blocks.caption: The governor's office said search and rescue efforts were underwayImage: Kadir Özen/DHA

blocks.text: Minister of Justice Akın Gürlek announced four public prosecutors have been assigned to the case.
'I thought it was an earthquake'
Eyewitness Nuri Ali Ulker described the blast as "very intense."
"The ground shook," he was quoted as saying by the state-run Anadolu news agency.
Another witness, Deniz Ulker, told the agency that the explosion "felt like the earth's crust was shifting beneath us. I thought it was an earthquake."
Turkey's big bet to become the new energy hub
The HABAS plant was established in 1987 and can produce 4.5 million tons of steel annually, according to the company's website.
Leftist opposition lashes out at the government
Turkey's leftist opposition party TIP lashed out at the government saying that the blast has once again laid bare how occupational health and safety are completely disregarded in the country.
The described the incident as "workplace homicide."
In an online post, TIP leader Erkan Bas said that "[t]he regime of bosses has declared war on the workers."
Union leader Basaran Aksu said that "the massacre calls for the resignation of the minister of labor."
He warned that "workers' blood" was being shed for profit.
According to the Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent NGO in Turkey, there were 226 workplace deaths reported across the country in September this year.

articles.title: Who is the suspected Chinese spy at centre of the Nvidia investigation?
articles.summary: Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman, had a close relationship with Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, reports say.

blocks.text: US chip giant Nvidia has said it is investigating reports that its CEO Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who had been the managing director of Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
The New York Times reported that US officials suspect Alice Huang has been working for China's spy agency to collect intelligence.
China has denied allegations of Huang being a Chinese spy, calling the allegations "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China."
Nvidia says it has no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised, but will "examine all available information".
Asia reporter Tessa Wong explains what we know about Alice Huang, and her links to Jensen Huang.

articles.title: Strait of Hormuz still a source of leverage for Iran
articles.summary: Attacks in the Strait of Hormuz put crews at risk and drive up energy shipping costs. Iran's ability to sustain them and the limits of US protection will shape how much trade can continue and at what…

image.caption: Latest data from the UKMTO show increased shipping traffic through HormuzImage: Atta Kenare/AFP

blocks.text: Since the Iran war started, attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz have put crews at risk of death and injury, forcing shipping companies to choose whether to attempt the passage or delay cargoes and face higher costs.

Merchant vessels continue to use the strait despite the danger but how long that can continue depends partly on Iran's ability to sustain its attacks and the United States' capacity to protect shipping and bear the cost.
Ali Mohammadi, an expert in Iranian affairs based in France, believes Iran's geography and the equipment it uses allow it to keep attacking ships.
But he sees the economic burden of the war as Tehran's main constraint.
"Iran's limitation in the Strait of Hormuz is economic rather than military, because continuing the war has a significant impact on its economy," he said.

It's unclear how long Iran can sustain attacks given the lack of reliable information on the nation's weapons stocks and its ability to replenish supplies. And sporadic attacks in the crucial waterway are also different from closing the strait completely.

"Even if a complete closure of the Strait of Hormuz were possible, it would not be sustainable because it could carry high political costs for Iran," Mohammadi told DW. "Iran cannot indefinitely disrupt its allies' access to the strait."
By threatening shipping, Iran can raise the cost of confrontation and seek leverage in negotiations but that may not guarantee success or yield concessions, the expert said.
Shipping crews caught in the crossfire of the Hormuz conflict
More crossings, but traffic remains depressed

Data from the UK Maritime Trade Operations Center's (UKMTO) weekly report, released on November 6, show 325 reported transits through Hormuz between October 29 and November 4. That was up from 277 the previous week, an increase of about 17%.
It's still roughly 65% below pre-war levels, the UKMTO assessed.
But vessel numbers alone cannot explain what is happening to energy supplies as cargo volumes and the routes used also matter, said Dalga Khatinoglu, an expert on Iran's energy and macroeconomics.

"If we look only at crude oil, Middle Eastern exports across all routes, from the Gulf of Oman and the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea, have largely recovered to pre-war levels," he told DW. "In some weeks in September and October, they even exceeded those levels."
His assessment covers the region's overall crude exports across all routes, not just shipments passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

The picture for refined petroleum products is different, Khatinoglu said. "Before the war, the Middle East exported about 6.2 million barrels of petroleum products a day. That figure has now roughly halved."

Liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports have also suffered. "As of September, exports from Qatar and the UAE were about 10% below pre-war levels. Although there has been some improvement, they remain severely disrupted," the expert underscored.
The cost of getting through spikes
Khatinoglu said recovering energy exports have not eliminated the costs associated with ongoing insecurity.
"Although oil exports from Middle Eastern countries have approached pre-war levels, shipping and insurance costs have remained very high," he stressed.

Citing recent figures from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), he said that average freight rates for a large tanker carrying crude from the Middle East to East Asia has risen about 12 times, from $3.18 (€2,84) per barrel at the beginning of the year to $37.13 a barrel at the end of October.
This means elevated costs for Asian importers even when crude is available.
Reducing costs and restoring commercial confidence in the safety of the strait requires more than a US military presence, Mohammadi said.
"There is only one solution to the Strait of Hormuz issue and that's an end to the war, accompanied by a lasting agreement that brings lasting security," he said.
Khatinoglu shared a similar view. "You cannot expect oil prices to return to pre-war levels simply by relying on US protection for ships in the Strait of Hormuz," he said.

articles.title: Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault convictions
articles.summary: The former comedian was found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others last week. The judge referred to Brand as a "predator."

image.caption: Russell Brand built his comedy career with jokes about his sexual exploitsImage: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/IMAGO

blocks.text: British media personality Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years and 6 months imprisonment on Monday after being found guilty of rape and assault.
He is required to spend at least two-thirds of that time in prison, and may be released under supervision after that if he displays good conduct while in jail.
Judge Joel Bennathan called Brand a "predator," and said that the sentence "just and proportionate...to the overall gravity of your criminality."
Bennathan also praised the "determination and bravery" of the survivors who came forward.
The 51-year-old had consistently denied the charges, brought about by six victims on allegations going back as far as 1999.
A jury of four women and eight men did not find his defense that all the encounters were consensual to be plausible, and found him guilty of raping or sexually assaulting four of his accusers.
Survivors, PM Burnham speak out
At the sentencing hearing, some of his victims gave victim impact statements to the court.

"I wanted ‌to express how this crime has affected me over the years," one woman said from behind a screen to protect her privacy, adding that the attack led to an "undeserved feeling of shame" she had carried for 20 years.
Another survivor called Brand a "sexual predator who has no remorse."

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham hailed the bravery of the survivors in a statement, and said his government would be "relentless in making whatever improvements we can” to provide more support for victims and make sure every police station has a sexual assault response team.
Who is Russell Brand?
Brand rose to prominence in the UK stand-up scene in the early 2000s with sets focused on his sex life, alcoholism, and heroin addiction.
He then became a presenter for several British televisions shows before starring in several Hollywood movies and being in a brief, high-profile marriage to American pop star Katy Perry.

As accusations of predatory behavior towards women began to mount, Brand left London and Hollywood behind for Florida. His politics changed from left-wing activism to promoting conservative ideas and conspiracy theories on his podcast.

He has said he underwent a religious conversion around this time. In 2016 he resumed his relationship with restauranteur Laura Gallacher, whom he first dated in 2007 when he was 31 and she was 19. They have since had three children together. Gallacher has remained by Brand's side throughout the court proceedings.
